scenes.heading: The Small-Files Problem & Compaction
scenes.narration: Let's take a deep look at The Small-Files Problem & Compaction and how it works under the hood in Spark.

scenes.heading: Why small files hurt
items: Each file costs metadata and a task
Reads become I/O and overhead bound
scenes.narration: The small-files problem arises when a job writes thousands of tiny output files instead of a few well-sized ones. Every file carries metadata overhead and typically maps to its own read task, so listing and scheduling costs balloon. On large tables this can overwhelm the driver's file listing and make reads dominated by overhead rather than useful I/O.

scenes.heading: How small files are born
scenes.narration: Small files usually come from having many partitions at write time, since each output partition produces its own file. Over-partitioning the output directory layout multiplies the problem by scattering data across countless folders. Streaming compounds it further, because each frequent micro-batch appends new small files. Recognizing these sources tells you where to intervene.

scenes.code:
# Control file count on write
(df.repartition(50)                 # target ~50 balanced files
   .write.mode("overwrite")
   .parquet("/out/table"))

# Or cap rows per file for even sizes
(df.write.option("maxRecordsPerFile", 1_000_000)
   .mode("overwrite").parquet("/out/table"))
scenes.heading: Controlling file count at write time
scenes.narration: Repartitioning to a modest count before writing produces that many balanced files instead of one per shuffle partition. Alternatively, maxRecordsPerFile caps how many rows go into each file, giving even sizes regardless of partition skew. The aim is files in the hundreds-of-megabytes range, large enough to amortize overhead but small enough for parallelism. Coalesce works too when you only need to reduce the count.

scenes.heading: Prevent vs compact
scenes.narration: The cheapest strategy is preventing small files at write time with repartition or a records-per-file cap. When a table already has a small-files mess, you compact it by reading the tiny files and rewriting them into fewer large ones, which Delta Lake automates with its OPTIMIZE command. Prevention is ideal, but periodic compaction is the practical cure for tables that accumulate small files over time, especially streaming sinks.

scenes.text: Aim for large, balanced files; prevent on write, compact on schedule.
scenes.narration: A simple periodic OPTIMIZE or rewrite job keeps read performance healthy on tables that would otherwise fragment.
